Probability & Statistics · Chapter 6

Chapter 6
Joint distributions

Lectures 15–16 · two unknowns at once: joint tables, independence, prediction from one quantity to another, covariance, correlation and sums

So far every model has had one unknown quantity: one count, one waiting time, one height. Most interesting questions involve two or more at once. How tall will a boy grow, given how tall his father is? If a geyser's eruption was long, how long until the next one? Does a second breathalyser reading tell us anything the first didn't? Are hair colour and eye colour connected? Each question asks how two random quantities behave together, and the tool for that is a joint distribution.

Joint distributions serve both of the course's goals. For prediction, they let us use one quantity to predict another: the father's height to predict the son's, the length of an eruption to predict the wait for the next. The best prediction turns out to be a conditional mean, and the way it shrinks towards the average is Galton's regression to the mean, seen at last through the mathematics. For inference, joint distributions describe how quantities are connected. Covariance and correlation measure the connection, and independence is the special case of no connection at all. But a connection in the data is not yet a cause, and this chapter keeps asking what produced the association.

Here is the route through the chapter.

  • Section 6.1 describes two random variables at once, with joint tables and joint densities.
  • Section 6.2 recovers each variable on its own (marginal distributions), and one given the other (conditional distributions).
  • Section 6.3 defines independence, the assumption behind most of the models so far.
  • Section 6.4 uses conditional expectation to predict one quantity from another.
  • Section 6.5 measures association with covariance and correlation.
  • Section 6.6 finds the mean and spread of sums and averages, which is the bridge to Chapters 7 to 9.

The calculus you need is double integrals over rectangles and simple regions (Section 0.4).

Think About It: Before You Start

A man is 6 ft 3 in tall, about 6 inches above the average for men. How tall would you predict his adult son will be: 6 inches above average, the average, or something in between? Write down a number before reading on. Example 6.9 answers it with Galton's data.

Something in between, and closer to the average than most people guess. Height is partly inherited, so the son of a tall father is likely to be tall. But the father's own height was partly luck: genes from his parents that he won't necessarily pass on, and a good childhood that his son may or may not share. The son gets only part of that advantage. In Galton's data, sons of fathers about 4 inches above average were only about 2 inches above average themselves. This is regression to the mean, and Section 6.4 shows exactly where it comes from.
